country.comment: Pilot experiment studied in Dhenkanal district in the state of Odisha, India.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF pp. 4–5, Section 2.2 & Figure 4

effect_estimate.comment: The paper reports qualitative institutional observations alongside descriptive tariff/operational comparisons rather than a quantitative statistical effect estimate on rural sanitation uptake.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative / descriptive case study — no statistical effect estimate reported for sanitation access. Formalizing the urban–rural partnership via a Memorandum of Agreement between Dhenkanal municipality and 17 gram panchayats reportedly increased rural households' access to faecal sludge management (FSM) services within a short period, reduced the rural distance surcharge by 50% (down from an informal market rate of 1.5–2 times the urban fee, where unsafe manual emptying had been nearly 50% cheaper on average), restricted the formal service radius to 10 km (down from up to 20 km informally, matched to ~50% spare daily capacity of the 27 kilolitres/day urban FSTP where rural households had been 13% of requests in Jan 2019–Feb 2020), and clarified broad roles while exposing gaps in non-contiguous village coverage, unsubsidized rural surcharges, and contractual accountability.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 8, Section 4.1 & Figure 6; PDF p. 10, Section 4.3; PDF pp. 11–12, Sections 5.1–5.2

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed; capped at 2 for non-experimental/non-quasi-experimental case study design). Through participatory practice research (2019–2021), the authors directly observed how formalizing an intermunicipal MoA, sizing a 10 km service area, negotiating a 50% surcharge cut, and lacking binding enforcement clauses operated on rural FSM service delivery.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary participatory/practice-research qualitative case study evaluating institutional planning, accountability, and financing challenges; while background planning drew on descriptive FSTP records and a 2020 household survey published separately ([13,14]), the empirical analysis in this paper is qualitative case-study observation and consultation without primary quantitative outcome testing (if the background survey/FSTP descriptive data were treated as a primary quantitative component, MMAT would be the alternative).

sample_size.comment: Single-district practice-research case study of Dhenkanal district (4 urban local bodies and 212 gram panchayats / 1237 villages), specifically the pilot partnership between 1 municipality and 17 gram panchayats; pre-partnership assessment conducted by the authors included a 1000-household survey (detailed in [13,14]), structured interviews with 8 sarpanches, and Jan 2019–Feb 2020 urban FSTP operational records.
sample_size.value: 1 pilot urban–rural partnership case (Dhenkanal municipality and 17 gram panchayats in Dhenkanal district); background assessment included a sample survey of 1000 rural households, structured interviews with sarpanches of 8 rural local governments, urban FSTP operational records (Jan 2019–Feb 2020), and stakeholder consultations

evidence_quotes.quote: We ﬁnd that the urban–rural partnership increased access to sanitation services among rural households within a short period, lowered service charges, and clariﬁed institutional responsibilities.
To inform the assessment, we conducted a sample survey of 1000 rural households and structured interviews with political leaders, or sarpanch(s), of eight rural local governments in 2020.
On ﬁnalization of the terms, the urban local government and 17 gram panchayats signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) to codify their partnership for service delivery on 28 December 2020.

Whatever resultant charge urban households pay, rural households pay a distance surcharge in addition to it—although the surcharge is 50% lower than what it was before the formalization of the partnership.
Before the partnership the municipality served rural households up to distances of 20 km, but the threshold was reduced to 10 km as part of the formalization.

Since the urban–rural partnership is framed as an agreement and not a contract, in its current form, it does not equip gram panchayats with any real leverage to hold its urban counterpart accountable for poor performance.
